messages.author: c9543c2fbdca30ad
messages.subject: another design question
parts:
Hello,

I am currently designing distance sampling methods in an attempt to=20
formulate density estimates of larval sucker fish in a deltaic wetland. =
I=20
am running in to a couple of issues that require guidance from people wit=
h=20
more experience with distance sampling than myself. Here is a brief=20
outline of the methods we've developed thus far:

For numerous reasons, including the dispersal of larval suckers in=20
response to the observer and the fact that larval suckers are extremely=20=

difficult to visually differentiate from larval perch and other non-=20
studied species, we believe that point transect sampling would be much=20=

more effective. Because there is a large tendency for larval suckers to=20=

disperse in response to the observer, recording objects in distance=20
intervals probably makes more sense than recording exact distances.=20=20=

Currently, we plan to sample a total of 60 points, selected through the=20=

use of a grid overlayed on top of the area to be sampled. There are four=
=20
different wetland types that will be used to stratify the data, and the=20=

number of points sampled per wetland type will be determined by the area=20=

of each wetland type.

Because visually observing larval suckers can only be done at short=20
distances, we are planning on making the intervals relatively small, with=
=20
the last interval before infinity, extending only 2.1m from the point.=20=
=20

My main question is in regards to actual observations. Because the botto=
m=20
substrate of the area we'll be sampling can be quite muddy, a certain=20
amount of time is needed before observations can start. Thirty plus=20
minutes might be needed for an observer to stand at the point before=20
beginning observations. I am wondering if some kind of device can be use=
d=20
that will allow for the response to the observer to be minimal, such as=20=

one in the attached document.

Simply, the device would be anchored to the bottom to a piece of rebar,=20=

then released after a certain time period to assure natural readjustment=20=

of suckers after the device had been placed. Once released it would floa=
t=20
to the surface, thus 'trapping' larvae in each distance interval, assumin=
g=20
that larval suckers are surface oriented. The observer would then stand=20=

on the point and record observed objects in each interval over a certain=20=

time interval. This device ensures that all larvae are observed in a=20
snapshot in time. This device would ensure no dispersal of larval sucker=
s=20
in response to the observer and would prevent movement, etc. My main=20
question is if a half-circle can be used as the sampling area? Because o=
f=20
the small distance intervals, it seems that this would be the most=20
effective way of observing.


Sorry this is so long, and thanks in advance for any suggestions/help.=20=
=20
Just let me know if you need more information about our sampling design,=20=

as I have only included a very brief synopsis. Thanks.

Charlie Erdman

=20

--

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: another design question
parts:
Charlie, the list doesn't accept attachments, so I can't see exactly
what you have in mind, but it sounds ingenious. A half-circle is fine.
You simply define a sampling fraction of one half, or alternatively
specify the effort at each point as one half. Of course, you have to
assume that the trap hasn't affected the habitat, so that fish densities
are representative.

Steve Buckland

If I understand correctly, the device would trap the fish in semi-circular
strips at increasing distance from the point. Would the trapped fish then be
counted exhaustively? If so, one would not expect the density of fish to
decrease with distance from the point. Also, if the fish are trapped in any

messages.subject: Re: another design question
parts:
Daniel, yes, I wasn't clear on this either, so I checked with Charlie
off the list. It seems the plan is for the observer to go to the point
as before (hence the use of a semi-circular grid, so the point is
accessible from one side). So some larvae will be missed in the outer
rings. I guess the question is whether this is more efficient than a
(smaller?) device that acts like a quadrat for plot sampling - which
could be gridded, so the larvae can't move over the entire quadrat while
being counted. The fish larvae are never actually removed from the
water - the grid just prevents them from changing their distance
interval from the point while they're being recorded. Hence the device
is to prevent responsive movement, but otherwise, the point transect
survey is conducted just as if there was no device (but over a
half-circle at each point).

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: another design question
parts:
Daniel, yes, I wasn't clear on this either, so I checked with Charlie
off the list. It seems the plan is for the observer to go to the point
as before (hence the use of a semi-circular grid, so the point is
accessible from one side). So some larvae will be missed in the outer
rings. I guess the question is whether this is more efficient than a
(smaller?) device that acts like a quadrat for plot sampling - which
could be gridded, so the larvae can't move over the entire quadrat while
being counted. The fish larvae are never actually removed from the
water - the grid just prevents them from changing their distance
interval from the point while they're being recorded. Hence the device
is to prevent responsive movement, but otherwise, the point transect
survey is conducted just as if there was no device (but over a
half-circle at each point).

Steve Buckland

Daniel Pike wrote:
> > Hi
> >
> > If I understand correctly, the device would trap the fish in semi-circular
> > strips at increasing distance from the point. Would the trapped fish then be
> > counted exhaustively? If so, one would not expect the density of fish to
> > decrease with distance from the point. Also, if the fish are trapped in any
> > case, why not just count them all and estimate density from the area covered
> > by the trap? Or perhaps I am misunderstanding something here.
> >
> > Good luck,
> >
> > Daniel Pike.

> >
> > On Mon, Feb 25, 2008 at 4:06 PM, Charles Erdman <cer...@tnc.org> wrote:
> >
> >
>> >> Hello,
>> >>
>> >> I am currently designing distance sampling methods in an attempt to
>> >> formulate density estimates of larval sucker fish in a deltaic wetland. I
>> >> am running in to a couple of issues that require guidance from people with
>> >> more experience with distance sampling than myself. Here is a brief
>> >> outline of the methods we've developed thus far:
>> >>
>> >> For numerous reasons, including the dispersal of larval suckers in
>> >> response to the observer and the fact that larval suckers are extremely
>> >> difficult to visually differentiate from larval perch and other non-
>> >> studied species, we believe that point transect sampling would be much
>> >> more effective. Because there is a large tendency for larval suckers to
>> >> disperse in response to the observer, recording objects in distance
>> >> intervals probably makes more sense than recording exact distances.
>> >> Currently, we plan to sample a total of 60 points, selected through the
>> >> use of a grid overlayed on top of the area to be sampled. There are four
>> >> different wetland types that will be used to stratify the data, and the
>> >> number of points sampled per wetland type will be determined by the area
>> >> of each wetland type.
>> >>
>> >> Because visually observing larval suckers can only be done at short
>> >> distances, we are planning on making the intervals relatively small, with
>> >> the last interval before infinity, extending only 2.1m from the point.
>> >>
>> >> My main question is in regards to actual observations. Because the bottom
>> >> substrate of the area we'll be sampling can be quite muddy, a certain
>> >> amount of time is needed before observations can start. Thirty plus
>> >> minutes might be needed for an observer to stand at the point before
>> >> beginning observations. I am wondering if some kind of device can be used
>> >> that will allow for the response to the observer to be minimal, such as
>> >> one in the attached document.
>> >>
>> >> Simply, the device would be anchored to the bottom to a piece of rebar,
>> >> then released after a certain time period to assure natural readjustment
>> >> of suckers after the device had been placed. Once released it would float
>> >> to the surface, thus 'trapping' larvae in each distance interval, assuming
>> >> that larval suckers are surface oriented. The observer would then stand
>> >> on the point and record observed objects in each interval over a certain
>> >> time interval. This device ensures that all larvae are observed in a
>> >> snapshot in time. This device would ensure no dispersal of larval suckers
>> >> in response to the observer and would prevent movement, etc. My main
>> >> question is if a half-circle can be used as the sampling area? Because of
>> >> the small distance intervals, it seems that this would be the most
>> >> effective way of observing.
>> >>
>> >>
>> >> Sorry this is so long, and thanks in advance for any suggestions/help.
>> >> Just let me know if you need more information about our sampling design,
>> >> as I have only included a very brief synopsis. Thanks.
>> >>
